articles.title: OpenAI's quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported, citing anonymous sources.
If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year.
OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said.
OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses.
But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion. OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has over a billion users, but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans.
Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth.
OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks.
OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon, said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October.
(Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.)
None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open source AI labs, especially those from China.

articles.title: Samsung Gallery now syncs with Google to back up your photos - Engadget
articles.text:
Samsung Gallery now syncs with Google to back up your photos
The company ended Gallery's Microsoft OneDrive integration back in September.
If you've ever owned a Samsung phone, you've most likely seen your device prompt you to back up your media to OneDrive at least once in the past. Back in September, however, Samsung removed its Gallery app's ability to sync with Microsoft OneDrive. Well, the phonemaker was likely cooking up another partnership behind the scenes, because it has just announced that its Gallery app can now sync with your Google account.
In the past, if you wanted to back up your photos and videos to your Google storage on a Samsung phone, you've had to use Google Photos instead of (or in addition to) your device's native Gallery app. With this update, you can stick to Samsung's Gallery app if you want to.The feature is currently only available on select Galaxy devices running One UI 9, Samsung's latest custom Android interface, but the company says it will roll out to more devices in phases. To enable the feature, tap the Cloud icon in Gallery or go to Gallery Settings and switch on Sync photos and videos.
Since the feature syncs media files to your Google account, you'll be able to access them in the Gallery app of another Samsung Galaxy device. Simply log into the same account on your other device and enable sync on it, as well. You'll then be able to see previews of your synced photos and videos on that device. If you want to access the original files, just select and download them. In case you want to do the opposite and remove files from your phone or tablet after they've been synced to Google storage, you can use Samsung's other new feature. It offers a Free up space option in the Sync photos and videos settings, which deletes original files from your device while keeping thumbnails visible in the Gallery app.
It's worth noting that Gallery sync will take up storage space on your Google account. Each Google account comes with 5GB of free storage by default, which you can expand to 15GB if you verify a valid phone number. If you want or need more than that, since that storage is shared across Google's services, you'll have to purchase a Google One subscription that will set you back $2 per month for 100GB of storage or $3 for 200GB.

articles.title: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.text:
Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. And it’s working.
Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 helped me track my fridge temperature and finally set up my in-wall speakers.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs, and a pair of RS-232 serial ports.
It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment.
All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development.
I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal.
But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad.
A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2.
I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help.
Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface.
In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again.
The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total.
I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem.
I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up.
Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV.
The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts.
That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point. The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged.
I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all.
But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

articles.title: London’s Fractile raises $720M for memory-first AI chips and hits $7B valuation
articles.text:
London-based chip designer Fractile has raised $720 million in a Series C round, betting that memory bandwidth, rather than raw computing power, is the main constraint holding back AI performance.
The funding values the four-year-old company at $7 billion, according to the Financial Times, which cited people familiar with the deal.
Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed, and Redpoint led the round. Other investors include Alphabet’s CapitalG, DST Global, BlackRock, Bain Capital Ventures, T. Rowe Price, Shopify Ventures, Balderton, the UK’s Sovereign AI fund, and the British Business Bank.
The valuation is a sharp jump from May, when Fractile raised around $220 million at a valuation of roughly $1 billion. The new figure puts it among the UK’s most valuable startups, alongside companies such as Revolut.
The Financial Times also reports that Anthropic has expressed interest in becoming an early customer for Fractile’s chips, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Founder Walter Goodwin’s argument starts with a growing imbalance between computing power and memory bandwidth.
Over the past 25 years, chip performance has increased roughly a millionfold, while memory bandwidth has grown only about 40 times. That leaves a 25,000-fold gap between the amount of data processors can calculate and how quickly they can access it.
Goodwin told the FT that today’s frontier models are “drinking through a straw”.
Fractile’s proposed solution combines custom DRAM and logic in a three-dimensional stack. The company says this architecture can deliver substantially higher bandwidth than high-bandwidth memory (HBM), while retaining enough capacity to run large models with long context windows. Goodwin claims it could make inference, the process of generating responses to user queries, up to 10 times faster.
Those performance gains have yet to be demonstrated in a production chip. Fractile has not released a commercial product, and its first chip is planned for next year. For now, the $7 billion valuation is based on its technology and prototypes rather than a product in the market.
The company is also trying to avoid a growing constraint in the AI supply chain. Many competing chipmakers rely on HBM to move data quickly between memory and processors.
The technology is expensive, and demand from AI companies is putting pressure on suppliers such as SK Hynix and Micron.
Fractile is entering an increasingly crowded market. Nvidia acquired Groq last year and launched its own inference chip in March, while startups including Etched, MatX, and fellow British company Olix are developing alternatives.
The opportunity, according to Thrive Capital’s Philip Clark, is an inference market that could soon become “at least as large as the market Nvidia is addressing today”.
He sees particular potential in AI agents, which need to run continuously for hours or days rather than respond to a single prompt.
The funding is also a significant moment for the UK’s effort to build domestic AI infrastructure. Goodwin described the government’s Sovereign AI fund as a driving force behind developing frontier AI technology from London.
Fractile also has offices in the US and Taiwan, however, and is building for a global market. Its next challenge is to turn its prototypes into working chips that can deliver the performance it has promised.

articles.title: Siri co-founder backs Helix for its voice ID tech | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For years, websites have relied on technology like CAPTCHA to prove that the user on the other end is human. More recently, social media platforms have turned to photos or videos to verify users’ identities. Now, a startup called Helix is betting that voice technology can do the same job, without requiring users to hand over sensitive personal information.
The voice technology, which can run directly on a user’s device, has attracted backing from Siri co-founder Dag Kittlaus, who will also act as an adviser.
The company raised $6.2 million in funding in a round led by Chicago Ventures, with participation from BAM Ventures, Aglaé Ventures, Corazon Capital, Press On Ventures, Tusk Ventures, Yonder Ventures, Rule 30, and Brown Angel Group.
The startup was founded by Alex Oberg, Anna Dorofiyenko, and Mike Hall in 2025. Oberg previously worked at Ticketmaster, which acquired his startup; Dorofiyenko led data science teams at Live Nation and Zillow; and Hall has worked at Nike and Tinder, where he helped develop the initial matching algorithm.
At Ticketmaster, Oberg played a role in creating Verified Fan, which is designed to keep bots out of the platform. As AI advanced, he started thinking along the same lines for a new solution.
“As AI started to come up in the last two years, I was realizing that it’s going to make it increasingly difficult to determine who’s human and who’s not on the internet. Identity on the internet’s always been about proxies for identity, right? It’s your email, it’s your phone, it’s your IP address, it’s your device fingerprint, it’s your device ID,” Oberg said.
He noted that with the rise of AI agents like Instinct and Muse, the industry needs to rethink human identity on the internet and rely on biometric signals like voice, which is where Helix comes in.
Its core technology can run directly on a device to determine whether someone is human and estimate their age. The company is also running pilots to explore whether voice can be used as a biomarker to detect conditions such as drunkenness or distress.
The company can deploy its technology to replace or supplement CAPTCHA and help block bot attacks. Helix said that because its model can run locally even on an iPhone 13, the cost of deploying the technology is minimal. The startup said one of its customers is Zeel, an in-home healthcare provider that uses Helix’s tech to verify the identities of providers visiting customers’ homes.
Oberg said verifying workers, such as cabdrivers, is another use case the startup is exploring. He also said that age-verification regulations for social media platforms around the world are forcing users to trade privacy for access. Helix’s voice technology, he said, could offer an alternative.
“There’s like an avalanche of regulation coming down because essentially society has decided children should not be able to use the internet as adults. That has created a bit of a strawman argument that everyone needs to trade their privacy for the sake of security and child safety. We are that company that’s saying, nope, don’t agree. It’s a four-second voice challenge,” he said.
The CEO also emphasized the limitations of Helix’s technology, noting that it cannot reliably detect whether someone is lying. He added that its voice technology doesn’t identify individual speakers — while verifying them being unique humans — and claimed that even if the company stores a voiceprint, it cannot be used to reconstruct a person’s voice.
AI-powered fraud is also a growing problem in phone calls. But Helix believes its technology isn’t yet capable of reliably detecting AI agents during live calls.
Siri co-founder Kittlaus said that voice-identification technology has finally reached a point where it works reliably, positioning Helix to scale as AI-powered fraud increases. He also said that Helix’s work to compress its models gives the startup a cost advantage.
“What folks at Helix are doing is, instead of teaching computers how to understand speech, these guys are understanding what the speech of the speaker actually means, what’s going on with them, if they are lying, are they impaired? That side of it is fascinating to me within the larger picture that I just described,” he told TechCrunch.

articles.title: What is the average lifespan of recordable Blu-ray discs? - Engadget
articles.text:
What is the average lifespan of recordable Blu-ray discs?
They can last you quite a while, but there are several factors to consider.
At this point, Blu-ray is a niche format, having mostly been supplanted by downloads, streaming and flash storage. But it's easily the format of choice for cinephiles, owing to higher ceilings on picture and audio quality. And if you want to archive files for a long time, Blu-ray may be more affordable, what with flash memory prices spiraling out of control.
How much can you trust recordable Blu-ray discs (BD-R), though? It's not an academic question if the files you're stashing are irreplaceable. If you make a bad decision, you could potentially lose your only digital copies of home videos, say, or a history of all your artistic projects.
Generally speaking, the news here is positive. BD-R may legitimately be your best option. There can be mitigating factors though, such as manufacturing quality, or simply having something to access the content on several years down the road.
How long can recordable Blu-ray discs last?
Short of accidents, the main threat to Blu-ray discs is something called disc rot. This is actually an umbrella term for various forms of decay. The reflective layer can gradually become oxidized, for example. Moisture might attract mold, or cause the layers of a disc to separate. Then there's the matter of exposure to UV (ultraviolet) light, though that's more likely to cause labeling to fade than harm your data. You can potentially notice rot before popping in a disc — look for signs like discoloration or spots.
According to Canadian Conservation Institute data, the cheapest BD-R discs will last five to 10 years on average. These should be avoided for any kind of archival project, since an external SSD is liable to last at least that long, and possibly several times as much while storing a lot more data. Remember, even the biggest BD-R discs top out at 128GB.
That said, manufacturing quality can have a huge impact. In better BD-Rs, a dye recording layer is replaced by a silicon and copper alloy, which you can tell if a disc appears dark gray or grayish-brown. Likewise, these discs might switch to a gold metal layer. The result, the CCI says, is double the lifespan at 10 to 20 years.
It gets better. BD-RE (rewritable) discs can conceivably last you as much as 20 to 50 years. That's so long that you might be able to pass them down to your children or grandchildren. On those timescales, however, other factors should probably discourage you from relying on Blu-ray.
Why BD-R discs might still be a bad idea for long-term storage
The most obvious reason is that discs are fragile. While storage in a relatively dry, dark and cool environment can deter rot, it's all too easy to accidentally crack or scratch a disc in a way that leaves it unreadable. Conversely, many external SSDs use tough metal enclosures that make physical destruction unlikely. All it might take to ruin your disc collection is forgetting that it's at the bottom of a moving box you're hauling, not the top.
Ultimately, the bigger issue might be industry support for Blu-ray. Optical drives have vanished as a default feature on computers, and companies are slowly pulling out the market for both external burners and BD-R discs, even Sony. At the moment, it's not that difficult to find burners and discs if you shop online. But there's no telling whether anyone will still be making this hardware 10 years down the road, much less 20. You could end up with an immaculately-preserved collection and no way of accessing it. Even your current drive might become useless if its software drivers cease to be compatible with later operating systems.
Whatever route you take, it's best not to be completely reliant on one storage medium for critical files. The general rule of thumb these days is to keep one copy in the cloud, and two others on separate forms of local storage. That's not always realistic — at the least, however, you should always be in a position to migrate your files to something fresher.

articles.title: United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
articles.text:
United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns.
United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
AI agents can’t attest that you don’t have explosives in your bags.
The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives.
While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf. The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal.
Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them. United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present. However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.”

articles.title: Vinhomes và Mitsubishi hợp tác toàn diện phát triển hạ tầng đô thị
articles.text:
Lễ ký kết diễn ra trong khuôn khổ Diễn đàn Công tư về hợp tác Kinh tế và Khoa học công nghệ Việt Nam - Nhật Bản do Chính phủ Việt Nam và Tổ chức Xúc tiến Thương mại Nhật Bản (JETRO) thực hiện nhân chuyến thăm Nhật Bản của Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm. Sự kiện đánh dấu bước tiến mới trong quan hệ hợp tác giữa Vinhomes và Mitsubishi Corporation, không chỉ trong lĩnh vực bất động sản mà mở rộng toàn diện sang ba trụ cột trọng tâm là nhà ở, hạ tầng và phát triển bền vững.
Cụ thể, về nhà ở, Vinhomes và Mitsubishi Corporation tiếp tục đẩy mạnh hợp tác phát triển các khu đô thị, đồng thời mở rộng sang bất động sản thương mại và phức hợp. Định hướng trên tạo nền tảng để hai bên phát huy thế mạnh, gia tăng nguồn cung chất lượng, đáp ứng các nhu cầu ngày càng đa dạng của thị trường.
Về hạ tầng, hai bên sẽ nghiên cứu các cơ hội hợp tác mới trong lĩnh vực logistics, khu công nghiệp, trung tâm dữ liệu, nền tảng trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) và công nghệ số. Đây là những lĩnh vực quan trọng trong việc nâng cao năng lực kết nối, thúc đẩy chuyển đổi số và hỗ trợ phát triển hệ sinh thái đô thị, công nghiệp hiện đại.
Về ESG và phát triển bền vững, Vinhomes và Mitsubishi Corporation thống nhất thúc đẩy ứng dụng công trình xanh, năng lượng tái tạo và tiếp cận các nguồn vốn xanh, qua đó góp phần hiện thực hóa mục tiêu phát thải ròng bằng 0 (Net Zero) của Việt Nam vào năm 2050.
Phát biểu tại lễ ký kết, bà Nguyễn Thu Hằng - Tổng Giám đốc Công ty Cổ phần Vinhomes cho biết: “Với sự tương đồng về tầm nhìn, định hướng phát triển cũng như năng lực quản trị và thực thi - Vinhomes và Mitsubishi Corporation sẽ cùng nhau kiến tạo nên những khu đô thị hiện đại, thông minh, kết nối thuận tiện và đáp ứng các tiêu chuẩn ESG quốc tế trong tương lai”.
Vinhomes và Mitsubishi Corporation đã thiết lập quan hệ hợp tác từ năm 2019, gắn liền với hành trình phát triển các đại đô thị đa trung tâm và các siêu đô thị của Vinhomes, cùng thúc đẩy chuyển đổi xanh, giảm phát thải carbon và hiện thực hóa mục tiêu Net Zero. Trong bối cảnh Việt Nam đang đẩy mạnh phát triển hạ tầng và đô thị xanh, thỏa thuận lần này không chỉ nâng tầm quan hệ giữa hai doanh nghiệp mà còn góp phần thúc đẩy dòng vốn ngoại vào nền kinh tế một cách bền vững.
| Mitsubishi Corporation là tập đoàn đa ngành hàng đầu Nhật Bản, hoạt động trong nhiều lĩnh vực kinh doanh như phát triển đô thị, giải pháp năng lượng, công nghiệp…, với mạng lưới 1.200 công ty trực thuộc phủ khắp 80 quốc gia. Mitsubishi Corporation đã tiến hành đầu tư tại Việt Nam từ năm 1991 đến nay, ghi dấu ấn với các thương hiệu như Mitsubishi Motors,... Vinhomes là công ty đầu tư, kinh doanh và quản lý bất động sản hàng đầu Việt Nam, đang triển khai khoảng 50 dự án trên toàn quốc, trong đó có 32 khu đô thị đã đi vào vận hành, phục vụ hơn 650.000 cư dân. Không chỉ tiên phong kiến tạo những khu đô thị đáng sống với quy hoạch chuyên nghiệp, tiện ích và kết nối đồng bộ, Vinhomes còn đi đầu trong việc phát triển các mô hình đô thị của tương lai như đại đô thị đa trung tâm và các siêu đô thị với quy mô lớn hàng đầu khu vực. | 
(Nguồn: Vinhomes)

articles.title: ElevenLabs moves beyond voice with custom models and a work app
articles.text:
ElevenLabs will help businesses fine-tune AI models on data from their own customer conversations, and opened early access to ElevenAI, an app that takes meeting notes. It also launched a partner programme and marketplace, and expanded its deal with Nvidia.
ElevenLabs will help businesses fine-tune AI models on data from their own customer conversations, the voice AI company announced at its New York summit on Wednesday. It also launched a workplace app, a partner programme and a marketplace.
In the coming months, firms can work with its researchers to tune its voice models and some open-source AI models. They can pick goals such as happier customers or fewer errors. The models then keep improving as more calls come in.
“Within a few years, conversational agents will become critical infrastructure for every enterprise, as essential as cloud or payments,” said CEO Mati Staniszewski.
ElevenLabs also previewed new features for ElevenAgents, its platform for voice and chat agents. Memory will let agents remember returning customers, such as one who prefers Spanish and can only talk after 5pm. Routines will handle follow-up work, such as calling back a mortgage applicant or offering a cancelled appointment to someone on a waiting list.
For staff, ElevenAI listens to meetings and turns them into notes and to-do lists. ElevenLabs says it asks for everyone’s consent before taking notes. Free early access opened on Wednesday.
It says it has more than 550 partners in 44 countries, including Google Cloud and Deloitte. It also signed a deal with McKinsey. From next year, firms can buy apps built by partners in its new marketplace.
ElevenLabs also expanded its deal with Nvidia, adding 15 MW of new computing power for large customers. The two are building a voice agent that calls patients with landlines for Poland’s national health booking system. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had been due to speak, pulled out of the event this week, as Nvidia’s board runs an inquiry into his conduct.
The push comes as ElevenLabs, valued at $22B in September with about $600M in revenue, faces cheaper rivals such as OpenAI’s voice models. Staniszewski said last week it could start preparing for an IPO in 2028.

articles.title: Grab giảm phí xuống 32%: cuốc xe 100.000 đồng, tài xế vẫn chỉ cầm về 59.680 đồng
articles.text:
Phí Grab giảm nhưng tổng khấu trừ vẫn có thể vượt 40%.
Ngày 10/11/2026, trần phí mới của Grab chính thức có hiệu lực sau cam kết với Ủy ban Cạnh tranh Quốc gia. Tổng phí nền tảng và phí sử dụng ứng dụng Grab được hưởng giảm xuống tối đa 32% giá trị hành khách thanh toán. Nhưng ở mức khấu trừ cao nhất, tài xế GrabCar chỉ thực nhận 59.680 đồng trên cuốc xe 100.000 đồng. Khoảng cách giữa hai con số này nằm ở các khoản thuế Grab thu hộ để nộp ngân sách.
Grab nói 32%, ứng dụng tài xế vẫn hiện hơn 40%
Trong thông báo ngày 5/11/2026, Grab viết: "Bản chất phần thu thực tế của Grab vẫn chỉ tối đa là 32%." Đây là phần phí nền tảng và phí sử dụng ứng dụng Grab được hưởng sau điều chỉnh. Mức phí được áp dụng linh động từ 7% đến trần mới và không bao gồm các khoản thuế hay phí thu hộ.
Cùng thông báo đó cũng thừa nhận tỷ lệ khấu trừ hiển thị trên ứng dụng tài xế có thể "lên tới tối đa 39,4% (với dịch vụ GrabBike) hoặc 40,3% (với dịch vụ GrabCar)". Doanh nghiệp giải thích: "Phần chênh lệch tương ứng là các khoản thuế thu hộ nộp về Ngân sách Nhà nước theo quy định." Như vậy, tỷ lệ hiển thị phản ánh tổng khoản bị trừ khỏi doanh thu chuyến xe chứ không chỉ phần Grab được hưởng.
Lấy một cuốc GrabCar có giá 100.000 đồng và không phát sinh phí cầu đường hay phí sân bay. Nếu Grab thu phí ở mức trần, nền tảng nhận 32.000 đồng. Tổng khấu trừ tối đa lên tới 40.320 đồng, trong đó 8.320 đồng là thuế thu hộ. Tài xế còn lại 59.680 đồng sau các khoản khấu trừ. Đây là mức sàn trong kịch bản chạm trần, không phải số tiền thực nhận của mọi cuốc xe.
Sau ngày 10/11, mức sàn của tài xế tăng thêm 7.680 đồng
Trước đợt điều chỉnh, phần Grab thu về trên mỗi chuyến GrabCar có thể lên tới 39,81%. Con số tương ứng của GrabBike là 40,60%. Theo cam kết mới, trần tổng phí nền tảng và phí sử dụng ứng dụng Grab được hưởng giảm xuống 32%. Riêng trần phí sử dụng ứng dụng giảm từ 28,76% xuống 25%.
Theo Bộ Công Thương, mức thực nhận tối thiểu của tài xế GrabCar tăng từ 52% lên 59,68%. Với cuốc xe 100.000 đồng, số tiền thấp nhất tài xế nhận được trước đây là 52.000 đồng. Sau điều chỉnh, mức sàn này tăng thêm 7.680 đồng. Đây là cải thiện thực tế về phần doanh thu tối thiểu tài xế được giữ lại.
Thông cáo của Ủy ban Cạnh tranh Quốc gia cho biết tài xế GrabCar hiện nhận từ 59,68% đến 84,31% giá trị hành khách thanh toán.
Dù vậy, tổng khấu trừ sau điều chỉnh vẫn có thể đạt 40,32% với GrabCar. Mức tương ứng của GrabBike là 39,41%.
Grab tự rà soát các chuyến xe từ năm 2024 đến nay. Khoảng 0,13% trong số đó có mức khấu trừ vượt 35%. Doanh nghiệp dự kiến bồi hoàn khoảng 3,9 tỷ đồng cho các trường hợp này. Ủy ban cũng thuật lại đề xuất của Grab dành khoảng 860 tỷ đồng cho các chương trình thưởng, hỗ trợ đối tác tài xế trong quý IV/2026. Ở Indonesia, quy định áp dụng từ 1/7/2026 giới hạn phí nền tảng ở mức 8% với xe ôm công nghệ hai bánh.
Người mua xe điện chạy dịch vụ cần tính lại thu nhập
Chênh lệch giữa tiền khách trả và tiền tài xế thực nhận càng đáng chú ý với người tham gia chương trình xe điện BYD của Grab. Chương trình áp dụng từ 7/9 đến 31/12/2026. Tổng mức đảm bảo thu nhập tối đa là 160 triệu đồng cho bốn kỳ. Mốc thấp nhất mỗi kỳ là 15 triệu đồng với tối thiểu 260 chuyến. Mốc cao nhất là 40 triệu đồng với tối thiểu 800 chuyến.
Grab nêu rõ: "Mức đảm bảo thu nhập là khoản thu nhập tối thiểu mà Bác tài sẽ nhận được nếu đạt đủ các điều kiện của chương trình". Thu nhập thực tế được xác định sau khi trừ phí sử dụng ứng dụng, thuế và những khoản khấu trừ khác.
Nếu mọi cuốc xe đều chạm trần khấu trừ và chưa tính thưởng, tỷ lệ thực nhận 59,68% cho một phép tính đáng chú ý. Để tài xế giữ lại 40 triệu đồng, tổng tiền hành khách thanh toán phải đạt khoảng 67 triệu đồng. Với mục tiêu thực nhận 15 triệu đồng, tiền khách trả tương ứng là khoảng 25 triệu đồng. Đây là kịch bản tính từ tỷ lệ khấu trừ, không phải điều kiện bắt buộc để được hưởng đảm bảo thu nhập. Nhưng nó cho thấy số tiền khách trả và khoản thu nhập ròng của tài xế không thể coi là một.
Việc Grab giảm trần phí xuống 32% là thay đổi có thật và đã nâng mức thực nhận tối thiểu của tài xế. Nhưng mức trần mới vẫn có nghĩa gần một phần ba mỗi cuốc xe thuộc về nền tảng. Cộng thêm thuế thu hộ, khoản tài xế bị trừ có thể vượt 40% trên màn hình ứng dụng. Tài xế cầm về chưa tới 60.000 đồng trên mỗi cuốc 100.000 đồng, không phải vì Grab thu vượt trần mà vì trần phí cộng với thuế vốn vẫn vận hành như vậy.
* Nguồn dữ liệu: Ủy ban Cạnh tranh Quốc gia, Bộ Công Thương, Grab Việt Nam và InfoPublik Indonesia.
* Mức thực nhận tối thiểu 59.680 đồng và mức tăng 7.680 đồng do Báo Công Thương tính từ thông tin Ủy ban Cạnh tranh Quốc gia công bố, đăng trên cổng thông tin Bộ Công Thương ngày 6/11/2026.
* Các phép tính 32.000 đồng, 40.320 đồng, 8.320 đồng, 39.810 đồng, khoảng 67 triệu đồng và khoảng 25 triệu đồng do Finelines thực hiện từ dữ liệu công bố.
* Ví dụ cuốc xe 100.000 đồng giả định không có phí cầu đường hay phí sân bay, các kịch bản thu nhập chưa tính thưởng.
* Số tiền khách phải trả ở khối 03 do Finelines tính theo tỷ lệ thực nhận sàn 59,68%, là kịch bản xấu nhất khi mọi cuốc chạm trần.

articles.title: iFixit teardown shows how Apple's glowing PROLED MacBook logo works - Engadget
articles.text:
iFixit teardown shows how Apple's glowing PROLED MacBook logo works
The new laptop goes the extra mile to recreate the iconic feature.
iFixit has shared its teardown of Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro and besides bemoaning the company's half-hearted commitment to user repairability, it also showed off the physical components that make the laptop's glowing logo work. The new lid design is one of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display's many charms, alongside its tandem OLED display and lighter weight.
Older LCD MacBooks featured a physical cutout that let the display's backlight illuminate the logo, but since OLED screens don't require backlights, Apple had to come up with a different solution to bring the design element back. iFixit found that the company uses a light strip with four LEDs layered behind the display, whose light is reflected through a diffuser to illuminate the logo. The Apple logo itself is also coated "like a two-way mirror," according to iFixit, so that it can appear metallic and reflective when the logo is off, but still let light through when the LEDs are on.
Apple ditched the glowing logo in 2016, so it's a bit ironic that the company waited until it stopped using backlit displays to bring it back. It used to be a cool bit of branding before, but now the company may see the glowing logo design as an important way to distinguish its most expensive laptop from the kind we peons are forced to use.
The rest of the internal changes to the laptop are more expected. Apple was able to achieve the new MacBook Pro's lighter weight by using less aluminum in the base and lid of the laptop and including a slightly smaller trackpad. The laptop's hinge was also reworked to make the display wobble less when you tap the screen. Those changes don't make it any easier to fix, though. The laptop is still complex to disassemble: For example, iFixit says that you have to remove the laptop's logic board to switch out its USB-C ports. Plenty of other components, like the MacBook's memory and the HDMI port, are also soldered in place. Anyone dropping up to $15,000 on a laptop probably isn't worried about doing their own repairs, but Apple's thin and light (and glowing) design comes with some tradeoffs, as always.

articles.title: Databricks' new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now perform multistep jobs that take extended work to finish. It does this through an ontology that Databricks built to give Genie the context it needs from the information that customers store on the Databricks platform.
Corporate leaders can now assign the agent a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them unsupervised, the company says. To prove the point, Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi showed me how he uses it internally. Instead of a product demo, he fired up his actual agent and walked me through his most recent chats and charts.
He showed me how it analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company didn’t score well, and how it helped him rate (and discard) fixes for those low scores that some executives suggested. He showed me how it summarized a big sales pitch to a prospect that went poorly — including the features the prospect said it needed before buying.
It also prepped him for a podcast interview by reviewing his previous appearances and developing likely questions. While we talked, he even had it tell him what he should say to me. (And its advice on that wasn’t bad.)
The fascinating part was that Ghodsi was using Genie to find the stuff that he’s now unlikely to hear as the big boss. It was a source of unvarnished truth about what wasn’t going well that he needed to address.
“Have you heard of Dunbar’s number? The magic number is 150,” he said when I pointed this out. Named for British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, it’s theoretically the maximum number of people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone, has direct relationships with them, and they feel safe to tell him negative info straight up.
With 12,000 employees, Ghodsi is the first to admit he can’t know everyone. At that size, a salesperson isn’t likely to confess a disastrous sales call to the CEO. An HR manager isn’t likely to confess that their idea for increasing employee satisfaction will probably fail.
“Anyone who has more than 150 employees, which is a lot of companies, a lot of people can get value out of this,” he said of AI agents generally and his product, Genie, specifically.
Ghodsi’s own use of Genie (often called dogfooding, from the phrase “eating your own dogfood”) is one reason why Databricks is now pitching it as an always-on agent for business leaders. He says he also uses it in his personal life, rather than a security-questionable alternative like OpenClaw or Instinct or Muse.
He believes Genie can do for the business side what AI, agents, and harnesses (the software that wraps around an AI model and lets it use tools) are doing for programmers. As for the risk that agents will ratchet up corporate AI costs, Ghodsi has an answer for that, too. He said costs can be controlled through Databricks’ Unity Gateway product. It allows companies to set usage limits and to swap in less expensive open-weight models.

articles.title: Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
articles.text:
Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.
Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
The proposed Digital Fairness Act seeks to bolster consumer protections for online users.
“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”
Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:
- A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.
- A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”
- Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.
- Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.
- Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.
- Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.
- Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.
- Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.
The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”
Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.
“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

articles.title: How to get this Siri camera upgrade for your iPad before its public release - Engadget
articles.text:
How to get this Siri camera upgrade for your iPad before its public release
You’ll be able to access Visual Intelligence from a new tab in the tablet's Camera app.
Apple users willing to install beta versions of its OS updates can get their hands on upcoming features sooner than most, as long as they're comfortable contending with the possibility of buggy software or apps breaking. And one such feature is the Siri Mode that's already available in the camera app on supported iPhones. It's also coming to compatible iPads as part of iPadOS 27.3 and will let you ask Siri AI questions about things you point your tablet's camera at.
We got our first look at this mode when Apple properly unveiled Siri AI at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June this year. It basically brings the company's Visual Intelligence tool for asking questions from photos to the camera app. But there's one distinguishing feature that's unique to iPads which isn't available on iPhones.
On iPads, Visual Intelligence includes Apple Pencil support. So, much like with Google's Circle to Search feature, you can snap a photo of something with your iPad, use your Apple Pencil to draw a circle around an item and learn more information about the object with the help of Siri AI.
It's worth noting that Visual Intelligence is already available on compatible tablets — iPad Pro and iPad Air with the M1 chip and newer, and iPad mini with the A17 Pro or A20 Pro chipset. As things stand, you can access it in the Camera app by long-pressing the Camera Control button or pressing the Action button if you've set it up to activate the feature (and your iPad has an Action button, of course).
In iPadOS 27.3, you'll have another way to access Visual Intelligence in the Camera app. All you'll have to do is swipe through the options in the viewfinder (i.e. photo, video and portrait modes) until you get to the Siri tab.
The company is expected to release the public version of iPadOS 27.3 in December. However, you can try it on your tablet right now, because Apple released the first beta in early November.
How to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta
To install the iPadOS 27.3 beta, open the Settings app on your iPad, then tap General > Software Update. If you haven't already done so, you'll need to enable beta updates. Tap the Beta Updates option, then iPadOS 27 Public Beta. After you go back to the Software Update tab, you should be able to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta.
Before you install the beta, it's best to create a full backup of your iPad using iCloud, a Mac or a Windows PC. Beta builds aren't the finished product, meaning they're more susceptible to bugs and errors. Backing up your data should be standard practice anyway, but it's especially advisable to do that before installing a beta version of an operating system, just to make sure your files and other information stay safe.
If you don't feel comfortable enough to install a iPadOS beta, that's perfectly fine! The public version of the OS update is likely coming soon. You can check out the Siri tab on your iPad's Camera app at that point.

articles.title: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI agents are all the rage, but they’re not quite as capable as their purveyors would have you believe.
Efforts to benchmark agents doing complex tasks show that they aren’t typically reliable enough to function without close supervision. LiveBench 2.0 shows Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeding on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks, respectively, and an effort by the AI infrastructure company EON to test agents in a simulated corporate environment found the most successful model tested, Claude Opus 4.8, performed tasks at 76.8% accuracy.
Now, a startup known as Plurai wants to boost those numbers with the same techniques that put self-driving cars on the street: Simulations using synthetic data based on a company’s own digital systems, meant to prepare models to tackle difficult edge cases.
Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software.
“The moment that we saw the wave of AI agents, we saw the same pattern: That it is very easy to build a demo, but [hard] to get something that will be reliable and cost effective,” Kadar told TechCrunch. “Since we saw the same pattern, the same pitch was that we want to build this simulation layer.”
On Wednesday, the startup said it had raised $13 million in seed funding to make that happen. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer.
Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments. When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple datasets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns.
To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor.
However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed the company’s models outperforming midtier frontier models at lower costs.
“We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said.
Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said.
Plurai hopes analogies between AI agents in physical and digital environments can prove predictive: While powerful general AI models are imbuing robots with fascinating capabilities, they aren’t yet reliable enough to be deployed widely. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data.
“My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said.

articles.title: Claude goes on by default for UK Copilot users from 9 December
articles.text:
Microsoft will switch on Anthropic’s Claude models by default for UK Copilot customers from 9 December, The Register reported. Anthropic processes that data in the US.
Richard Speed wrote for The Register that UK organisations with no setting chosen by then will have Claude enabled. Administrators can still turn it off. Leaving the setting untouched means opting in.
Anthropic works as a Microsoft subprocessor, a third party that handles customer data under Microsoft’s contracts and oversight, according to Microsoft’s Copilot documentation. Claude is already on by default for most of Microsoft’s commercial customers. The EU, the European Free Trade Association and the UK have so far been the exceptions.
“This affirms Microsoft’s commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance,” Microsoft wrote.
Outside the EU Data Boundary
The same documentation says Claude models in Copilot fall outside Microsoft’s EU Data Boundary. They are also excluded from in-country processing commitments. The UK is not covered by the EU Data Boundary, so Microsoft is changing the default there, according to The Register.
The change covers Claude in Copilot, Researcher, Copilot Studio, Power Platform and Copilot in Microsoft 365 apps. Microsoft is also retiring a setting that limited Claude to Microsoft 365 apps.
Some advanced Anthropic models, such as Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, stay off by default everywhere. Anthropic keeps data from those models, mostly for up to 30 days, so administrators must opt in to them separately, Microsoft said.
The same week, Anthropic launched Claude Sheets and other office tools that compete with Microsoft’s own.
Whitehall’s US tech bill
The UK public sector’s dependence on US technology is the subject of a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR). Less than £1 in every £6 spent with the 150 largest technology suppliers stays with British companies, The Register reported on Wednesday.
About 42.5% of that spending appears to go to UK companies. The share falls to 15.4% once the researchers looked past headquarters to ownership, staff and resellers. The US gets the most, with £9.2bn of the £19.2bn spent with the largest suppliers.
The report, called Locked In, found that AI often reaches government through existing cloud and software deals. NHS England’s Copilot rollout reached 505,000 staff. It ran under a national licensing deal signed in June 2023, before Copilot was generally available.
IPPR also pointed to US restrictions on Anthropic models. It cited limits on early access for the UK’s AI Security Institute too.
The government has committed £500m to a Sovereign AI Fund. IPPR wants Whitehall to buy technology as a single customer and make it easier to switch suppliers. It also wants the UK to work with France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea on access to advanced AI.
“But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can’t be our only bet,” said Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR.
UK administrators who want to keep Claude switched off in Copilot have until 9 December to change the setting.

articles.title: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
articles.text:
Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.
Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Toyota is reviving the Scion badge as an experimental mobility incubator—starting with an Indiana-built, 25-mph kei truck engineered for American fleets.
Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan, telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.
Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016, would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.
When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.
It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.
The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.
Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.
Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.
Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.
To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.
Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.
The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.
Images by Toyota

articles.title: Đà Nẵng có thêm đầu mối trung chuyển hàng hóa hơn 8,6ha
articles.text:
Ngày 10/11, Tổng Công ty Cổ phần Bưu chính Viettel (Viettel Post) ra mắt Trung tâm Logistics Viettel Đà Nẵng tại Khu công nghiệp Liên Chiểu.
Phát biểu tại sự kiện, Chủ tịch UBND TP Đà Nẵng Nguyễn Mạnh Hùng cho rằng trung tâm không chỉ có ý nghĩa đối với hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh của Viettel mà còn góp phần hiện thực hóa định hướng phát triển logistics của thành phố.
Chủ tịch TP Đà Nẵng nhìn nhận, sau khi hợp nhất với tỉnh Quảng Nam, thành phố có điều kiện tăng cường kết nối giao thông liên vùng, từng bước hình thành mạng lưới sản xuất và lưu thông hàng hóa quy mô lớn, có sức cạnh tranh.
Đà Nẵng có cảng biển, sân bay quốc tế và lợi thế kết nối Hành lang kinh tế Đông - Tây với các tỉnh miền Trung, Tây Nguyên. Tuy nhiên, theo Chủ tịch UBND thành phố, những lợi thế này chỉ phát huy hiệu quả khi địa phương tổ chức được các dòng hàng hóa, thu hút doanh nghiệp và hình thành dịch vụ logistics chất lượng, góp phần giảm chi phí cho nền kinh tế.
Ông Hùng nhấn mạnh, chi phí sản xuất, vận hành và vận chuyển có ảnh hưởng trực tiếp đến sức cạnh tranh của hàng hóa. Khi chi phí hợp lý và thời gian lưu thông được rút ngắn, doanh nghiệp sẽ có thêm điều kiện mở rộng sản xuất, tiếp cận thị trường và nâng cao hiệu quả đầu tư.
Vì vậy, phát triển logistics không chỉ dừng ở đầu tư kho bãi và dịch vụ vận chuyển mà trở thành bộ phận quan trọng trong phát triển kinh tế, góp phần nâng cao năng suất lao động, giảm chi phí, nâng cao sức cạnh tranh. "TP Đà Nẵng cần một hệ thống logistics hiện đại, đủ năng lực đáp ứng yêu cầu phát triển trong những năm tới", ông nói.
Trung tướng Tào Đức Thắng, Chủ tịch kiêm Tổng Giám đốc Tập đoàn Viettel, cho rằng đầu tư cho logistics không chỉ là đầu tư vào hạ tầng và dịch vụ mà còn góp phần nâng cao năng lực cạnh tranh, tạo nền tảng cho phát triển dài hạn.
Theo ông, việc đưa Trung tâm Logistics Viettel Đà Nẵng vào hoạt động sẽ góp phần tăng cường liên kết vùng, thúc đẩy lưu thông hàng hóa và bổ sung năng lực logistics cho Đà Nẵng, khu vực miền Trung và cả nước.
Trung tâm Logistics Viettel Đà Nẵng có khu nhà kho và hạ tầng phụ trợ rộng khoảng 39.300m2, tích hợp 7 nhóm công năng, từ lưu kho, hoàn tất đơn hàng, gom hàng, điều phối vận tải đa phương thức đến logistics xuất nhập khẩu, kết nối hải quan, dịch vụ giá trị gia tăng, logistics thương mại điện tử và điều hành số.
Nằm cách cảng Liên Chiểu khoảng 1km, trung tâm kết nối với quốc lộ 1A, cảng Tiên Sa và sân bay quốc tế Đà Nẵng. Công trình được định hướng làm đầu mối gom hàng từ các vùng sản xuất trong khu vực và từ Lào qua cửa khẩu Lao Bảo trước khi đưa đi xuất khẩu; đồng thời tiếp nhận, phân phối hàng hóa đến các trung tâm tiêu thụ trong nước.

articles.title: IBM plans to link two quantum chips into a 1,040-qubit system in 2027
articles.text:
IBM’s next quantum chip, Nighthawk r3, is designed to run 10,000 operations on 520 qubits. IBM plans to link two of them into a 1,040-qubit system in 2027. Customers report speedups of up to 19x on the current Nighthawk chip.
IBM plans to build a quantum computer with more than 1,000 qubits in 2027 by linking two of its next-generation chips, the company announced on Wednesday.
The new chip, called Nighthawk r3, is designed to run 10,000 quantum operations on 520 usable qubits. It has 10 connectors for joining chips together. IBM says two of them will form a single 1,040-qubit system.
Qubits are the basic units of a quantum computer. Each run of a quantum program gives one result, so useful work can take millions or billions of runs. That makes speed as important as size.
“Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental,” said Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research.
The current chip, Nighthawk r2, launched in September. It can produce up to 100,000 results per second on 120 qubits. IBM says customers and partners have run 34 billion programs on it, with speedups of up to 19x over its older Heron chips.
German energy firm E.ON reported a 15x speedup on work to optimise power grids. IBM also says it has linked earlier Nighthawk chips at 99.3% accuracy, short of its 99.9% goal. Linking chips is one of the hardest scaling problems in quantum computing.
All of the figures come from IBM and its partners. IBM still aims to deliver its first error-corrected quantum computer, Starling, by 2029, Live Science reported last year.
IBM is also hedging its bets. It agreed to buy HRL Laboratories, which builds silicon qubits, in July. In October, DARPA moved IBM to the final stage of its quantum testing programme, while rival Quantinuum raised $1.68B in its June IPO.

articles.title: Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
articles.text:
Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more.
Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
Tabletop provides customizable, collaborative spaces for all your personal planning needs.
“Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.”
Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist, and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.

articles.title: Helsing Clarity aims to ‘connect what is seen to what is struck’
articles.text:
German defence company Helsing has launched Clarity, a direct challenge to Palantir. The AI platform helps armed forces turn drone, satellite and sensor data into targets. Helsing says it builds the software in Europe, under European control.
Clarity pulls in sensor feeds, open sources, written reports and the systems a unit already runs. It finds military assets and positions across them and shows them to a human for review. It then prepares the information a weapon needs, Helsing said in a statement on Wednesday.
Reuters reported that Palantir’s Maven leads this market. Maven already sits inside Pentagon and NATO workflows. Helsing did not disclose whether any military already uses Clarity, or when it expects it to enter service.
“All armed forces need an intelligence capability that keeps pace with the fight. Autonomous systems play an increasingly important role. It is therefore important to connect what is seen to what is struck,” said Gundbert Scherf, Helsing’s co-CEO and co-founder.
Hundreds of agents, one human in charge
Helsing Clarity runs hundreds of AI agents built for military use, the company said. They share one military ontology, a common map of how the data fits together, and one evidence base. Helsing trained the models on real operational data, synthetic data made by AI and simulated environments.
The company said humans stay in command. An operator reviews the evidence, selects each asset to engage and authorises every hand-off to a weapon. Clarity nominates a target only when independent sources agree, confidence is high and an operator confirms. Clarity records every decision with the name of the person who made it.
The platform runs on infrastructure the customer owns. It follows NATO standards and the modular open systems approach (MOSA), so it can connect to weapons from any maker.
Europe wants its own tools
Helsing is pitching Clarity at European governments that want control over their military software. France’s domestic intelligence service is already dropping Palantir for a homegrown tool. France and Germany have also pledged to build a European rival.
In the UK, Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software to GP records, the Guardian reported. The campaign group Foxglove obtained the WhatsApp messages under the Freedom of Information Act. Palantir’s £330m contract to run the NHS data platform excludes GP data. Palantir told the Guardian that it is for the government to decide how to roll out the software.
Palantir turns to the Democrats
In Washington, Palantir is preparing for a Democratic-controlled Congress. Chief executive Alex Karp spoke to Politico’s Playbook on Wednesday, a week after the midterm elections.
“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far left environment,” Karp told Politico.
He said all of Palantir’s products are “essentially progressive”. Karp also said Trump had mishandled immigration enforcement, which Palantir’s ImmigrationOS software supports under a $30m contract, according to Politico.
Politico reported that Palantir has hired Jon Tester, a former Democratic senator from Montana, as an adviser. The company faces possible congressional investigations. Democratic lawmakers have asked whether Palantir’s work with the Department of Homeland Security enables surveillance of Americans. The company has denied conducting or enabling mass surveillance.
“Be transparent, be forthright, address the question straight up,” Tester said of his advice to Karp.
A Palantir executive for CISA
On Monday, President Donald Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). CISA is the US civilian cyber defence agency. LoSapio has been Palantir’s chief information security officer since September 2024.
CISA has had no Senate-confirmed director since Jen Easterly left in January 2025, Nextgov/FCW reported. Its workforce has shrunk by about a third. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before this Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again. The new Senate will have a Democratic majority.
